opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most important strategic questions we wrestle with, and honestly the answer has shifted over time. Early on, when you're trying to get a humanoid walking and doing useful work, there's a strong pull to build everything yourself, because the supply chain for this form factor just didn't exist. Nobody was making actuators with the torque density, the backdrivability, and the size constraints you need for a knee or a hip on a bipedal robot. So you end up designing your own motors, gearboxes, and motor drivers simply because there's no alternative.

The way I think about it now is basically: where is the differentiation, and where is the risk? If a component directly determines performance — actuators, the hands, the core control electronics, and the software stack that ties it together — that's where we want deep in-house expertise, because that's where the robot either works well or it doesn't. Owning those lets you iterate fast. If you want to change a gear ratio or tweak a thermal design, you don't want to wait on a supplier's roadmap.

But there's a huge category of things where vertical integration just slows you down and burns capital. Batteries cells, standard sensors, bearings, fasteners, compute modules, cameras — there are mature industries that do those at scale and at a cost you can't touch. Trying to reinvent those is a distraction.

The other piece is manufacturing scale. Designing a part in-house doesn't mean you have to fabricate it in-house. A lot of what we do is own the design and the IP, then partner with contract manufacturers who know how to make millions of precision parts. That gives you the control without having to stand up a whole factory for every subsystem.

And I'd say the line keeps moving. As the humanoid industry grows, suppliers are starting to build components specifically for this market, especially in actuators and hands. So something you had to build yourself three years ago, you might be able to buy in two years, and that frees your engineers to focus on the next hard problem. The goal is to stay vertically integrated on what makes you better, and be very pragmatic about everything else.

r001.rationale: The response says suitable humanoid actuators were unavailable early on, but does not identify suppliers’ limited production capacity as a reason to manufacture parts in-house.

r002.rationale: It mentions buying standard components, but does not explain how using common components allows robots to be produced in different product tiers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that it's not a fixed philosophy, it's a moving line, and where it sits depends on what stage the company is at and what actually differentiates the product.

The way I frame it internally is: build what makes you different, buy what makes you the same. For a humanoid, the things that make you different are the actuators, the hands, the control software, and the way the whole system is integrated. Those are the things where off-the-shelf parts either don't exist at the performance you need, or they exist but they're sized for a different application, like industrial arms or e-bikes, and the compromises show up immediately in weight, backdrivability, thermal behavior, cost. So early on, we ended up designing a lot more in house than we wanted to, not because we loved doing it, but because the supply base for humanoid-grade components basically didn't exist yet.

But there's a trap there. Vertical integration feels good because you control everything, and then you wake up one day and you're running a motor company, a gearbox company, a battery company, and a robot company, and you're mediocre at three of them. Every one of those you take in house is engineering headcount and capital that isn't going toward the thing customers actually pay for, which is a robot that does useful work reliably. So we try to be pretty disciplined about asking: is this a true differentiator, or is it just that nobody sells it yet?

Those are different answers. If it's a true differentiator, you build it and you keep building it. If it's just a gap in the supply chain, you build it as a stopgap, but you design your interfaces so you can swap in a supplier part the moment one shows up that's good enough. And that's happening fast. Three years ago you couldn't buy a decent frameless motor at humanoid scale without a custom program. Now there are several vendors, and the Chinese supply chain in particular is moving very quickly on actuators and sensors. The smart move is to let them commoditize that layer and ride it.

The other thing I'd say is that the calculus flips as you scale. At a few dozen units, in-house manufacturing is fine, you can hand-build and hand-tune. At thousands of units, yield, consistency, and cost per part dominate, and that's where a mature supplier with real process control beats a small in-house shop almost every time. So part of the question isn't "do we make it or buy it," it's "do we make it now and transition it later," and planning for that transition up front rather than getting surprised by it.

Where I'm still firmly on the build side is anything touching safety-critical control and the compute and software stack. You can't outsource your understanding of how the system fails. Everything else is negotiable.

r001.rationale: It cites the lack of suitable humanoid-grade parts in the supply base, but does not identify suppliers’ limited production capacity as a reason to manufacture parts in house.

r002.rationale: It discusses differentiating components and commoditized parts, but does not explain that common basic components still allow manufacturers to make robots in different product tiers.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be very deliberate about what you own. If a supplier can make a component reliably, at the right cost and to the specifications you need, there’s a strong argument for buying it. Building everything yourself adds complexity, and it can distract you from what actually makes the robot useful.

But if a component is limiting performance, or it’s so tightly connected to your design that you need to iterate on it constantly, then bringing it in house can make sense. You want control over the things that differentiate the product.

And that balance changes as you scale. What works for ten robots may not work for ten thousand. So I’d look at performance, cost, supply reliability, and how quickly we need to make changes. The goal is to build a robot that works reliably at a price customers can justify.

r001.rationale: The response mentions supply reliability and scaling, but does not identify suppliers’ limited production capacity as a reason to manufacture parts in house.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain how using common basic components can still allow manufacturers to offer different robot product tiers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be very deliberate about what you make yourself. If a supplier can give you a component that meets your performance, cost, and reliability requirements, there’s a strong argument for buying it. You don’t get extra credit for making every part of the robot.

But where a component really determines what your robot can do, or where the available options force you into compromises, that’s where bringing development in house can make sense. And you have to think beyond the prototype. Can you get that part consistently? Can you service it? Can the supplier scale with you?

So for me, it’s less about being vertically integrated as a philosophy and more about owning the things that differentiate the product, while using suppliers wherever they help you deliver a reliable robot at a price customers can justify.
